#3512. Marvel’s Newest Superhero Was Created to Solve a Major Magic: The Gathering Problem

Magic's VP of design talks about Darkhold Destiny's secret new hero

Marvel has no shortage of superheroes. But when Magic: The Gathering designers started assembling the cast of Marvel: Darkhold Destiny, they discovered that even decades of comic book history couldn’t quite give them everything they needed. And what they needed was more green. The solution was to create an entirely new Marvel character.

In an interview with Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta, Magic vice president of design Aaron Forsythe talked about the unique approach that Marvel and Wizards of the Coast are taking for the game’s third crossover set, specifically about the development of a unique character that will feature prominently in Darkhold Destiny and the accompanying Marvel Comics.

“The idea for a unique character was Marvel’s,” Forsythe says when asked outright about the new character, who is named Fraxi. “I will say that she’s a green card.”

That might sound surprising in a universe that includes the Incredible Hulk, but Forsythe meant something deeper than gamma-irradiated skin. Magic divides its characters, spells, and gameplay philosophies across five colors with distinct identities that define much of the game. Finding recognizable characters who fit green’s combination of nature, instinct, and growth can be a challenge when adapting another franchise.

“It’s a tough color in a lot of Universes Beyond sets because there are not many bestial or druidic characters,” Forsythe says. “But there are plenty of red, blue, white, and black characters throughout all sorts of IPs. Green’s always a little bit more of a stretch, the way Magic defines the ethos and power suite of green.”

In developing Darkhold Destiny, Marvel pitched the idea for the Magic team to design a unique character for the set that would join Marvel canon. In the set's unique storyline, Dormammu and Hela combine a page from the Darkhold to rip open the walls between realities, unleashing arcane nightmares across the Multiverse. Thor and Doctor Strange are positioned as the main heroes, but a third brand-new hero will seemingly join them. According to Forsythe, making that character aligned with green in the game emerged as a focus.

“That way, it would really help us flesh out our roster in a way that feels authentically Magic,” Forsythe says.

In recent weeks, listings for some Magic accessories, including a deck box and playmat, identify a character named "Fraxi, Scion of Yggdrasil." When Polygon brought up the name and suggested a connection to the World Tree, Forsythe declined to elaborate. “I will not contradict what you’re saying,” he admits.

According to a blog post from principal designer Mark Rosewater, “Scion” as part of a creature’s name essentially just means they are a “descendant” or heir of something. For someone associated with Yggdrasil, that means that Fraxi could be the World Tree’s offspring, an embodiment of its power, or someone chosen to inherit that power. None of this is confirmed by any means, but it raises interesting possibilities about the nature of Fraxi and her power. Is she the physical embodiment of Yggdrasil, created to defend the various worlds it is a part of? Is she literally Yggdrasil’s avatar, or merely a character empowered by the World Tree in the same way that plenty of other Marvel characters are chosen to wield a cosmic entity's power?

In Marvel’s cosmology, Yggdrasil is the World Tree associated with Asgard and the other realms of Thor’s mythological corner of the universe. That makes it a particularly meaningful connection for Darkhold Destiny, whose story involves an invasion across dimensions.

At an October press event attended by Polygon, narrative set lead Dillon Deveney explained that after Hela and Dormammu use the Darkhold to launch their conquest, the ensuing conflict spans more than two dozen dimensions, including the 10 realms of Marvel’s Norse mythology. A character tied to the tree connecting those realms would have an obvious stake in their survival — and potentially a useful role in defending them.

That probably feels familiar to longtime Magic players. The game’s Norse-inspired setting, Kaldheim, has its own World Tree connecting its realms. That’s distinct from Marvel’s Yggdrasil, but the shared imagery makes Fraxi’s apparent premise an especially natural fit for the crossover. Deveney’s account of her creation also suggests that her role goes beyond filling a gap in the color pie. While developing the story, he kept encountering a role that existing Marvel characters didn’t quite fit.

“There was an obvious hole,” Deveney told Polygon in October. “I found myself forcing other characters into this role.”

The team developed roughly five different character concepts and sent them to Marvel. One, Fraxi, prompted a particularly enthusiastic response.

“They came back really fast, and they were like, ‘I don’t know how you guys knew, but this one, we’ve been looking for a character like this for a while,’” Deveney recalled.

Her origin story will be told in a Darkhold Destiny comic written by Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly. The first chapter will be released digitally on Feb. 26, 2027, with a physical release planned to coincide with the launch of Magic's Darkhold Destiny set on April 9. For now, Fraxi looks poised to give Marvel a new connection to its World Tree — and give Magic the kind of nature-powered hero its designers were struggling to find for Universes Beyond.

I knew Spider-Man: Brand New Day would make a ridiculous amount of money when it landed on this summer's 2026 movie schedule. What I didn't expect was to hear Sony's top movie executive making a serious case for Tom Holland's latest superhero adventure to earn a Best Picture Oscar nomination. But here we are, and apparently, the studio is prepared to put some real effort into making it happen.

Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group chairman and CEO Tom Rothman recently spoke with Variety about the movie's extraordinary success and why he believes it deserves Academy voters' consideration. With Brand New Day earning roughly $2.5 billion worldwide and breaking the domestic box office record, Rothman thinks there's something special about how audiences connected with Peter Parker's story. He explained:

The reason it did as much business as it did is not because it's a superhero movie, it's because it's a super person movie.

I actually get what he's saying. While I enjoyed the action in Brand New Day, what stuck with me was how much of the movie focused on Peter's loneliness after the events of No Way Home. Here's a guy who can swing between skyscrapers and take down some of Marvel's most dangerous villains, but he can't get the people he loves to remember who he is. That's a pretty miserable situation, even by Peter Parker standards.

Audiences clearly responded as well. The film received overwhelmingly positive reviews. It also became the highest-grossing movie in North American box office history, an accomplishment I imagine Sony will mention quite a bit over the next few months. But does all that mean it deserves an Oscar nomination?

Rothman certainly thinks so. When asked whether or not a strong box office means Brand New Day should be a Best Picture contender, he responded:

Once upon a time there were five best picture nominations, and then it was expanded to ten, to try to make room, I think, for quality commercial filmmaking… we’re biased, but we think [it should be nominated] so. We hope people will think about it.

Sony is backing up those comments with an actual campaign. According to Deadline, the studio has hired awards consultants and is planning special screenings and filmmaker Q&As beginning ahead of Thanksgiving. There's also talk of a theatrical rerelease designed to put the movie back in front of audiences and Academy voters.

Of course, superhero movies have historically struggled to crack the Best Picture category. Black Panther earned a nomination in 2019, followed by Joker the next year, but neither won. Even Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight missed a Best Picture nomination, despite earning eight Oscar nods and winning two.

As for Spider-Man, the character, he hasn't exactly been an Academy favorite. Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2 won Best Visual Effects in 2005, while Into the Spider-Verse took home Best Animated Feature in 2019. Although no movie starring the web-slinger has ever competed for Best Picture.

Still, I can understand Rothman's reasoning. Director Destin Daniel Cretton made a movie that made room for surprisingly intimate character moments, even amid all the enormous superhero spectacle. CinemaBlend's Jerrica Tisdale previously explained why that balance made the movie work so well, and I think it's a fair argument. Whether Academy voters agree is another matter entirely.

The nominations for the 99th Academy Awards will be announced Jan. 21, 2027, and Brand New Day will have some stiff competition. After watching what Sony and Marvel accomplished with Peter Parker this summer, I'm certainly not going to dismiss the idea outright. Besides, if anybody deserves a little recognition after everything he's been through, it's Peter Parker. The poor guy could use a win.

#3510. Clint Eastwood's Frustrations With His Aerial Thriller Were Solved By A Legendary Artist

When Clint Eastwood made his 1982 jet-based thriller "Firefox," he had a great deal of trouble with the aerial special effects. The film includes many shots of high-speed aircraft, all of them filmed against sky-colored backgrounds or snowy climes, and Eastwood had trouble eliminating the hard dark matte lines that result from piecing such special effects shots together on a physical film strip. Luckily, Eastwood was able to employ John Dykstra, the Academy Award-winning special effects man from "Star Wars," to help solve the problem.

In a behind-the-scenes documentary about "Firefox," Eastwood voiced his complaints about the matte problems he had with the plane scenes in "Firefox," alluding to the fact that earthbound planes are harder to visually realize than, say, spaceships. Matte lines in starship scenes, you see, can be hidden in the blackness of space. Dykstra was also interviewed in the same documentary, and he explained that the VFX for "Firefox" were more difficult than "Star Wars" "by a factor of ten" because of the matte problem.

Dykstra was enthused to share his techniques on how he filmed the fast-streaking sky required for fast-moving plane scenes, as he was able to achieve the effect by using a very slow-motion camera — very, very slow-motion, clicking off "a frame or two" every second — while shooting footage of the sky in a Learjet that was traveling 350 miles per hour. Most film cameras shoot at 24 frames per second, so Dykstra noted that filming in such a way forced them to cover a lot of physical space very quickly.

The passing mention of a "matte line" might confuse a VFX layperson, so luckily Dykstra explained succinctly what a matte is. In Dykstra's words, a matte is "a combination of two pieces of film on to one, [to] make them look like they were shot at the same time." When two pieces of film are combined in the way Dykstra describes, a black line, or a matte line, forms around the plane or the starship in question.

"Firefox" is about a high-tech Soviet superplane, the fictional MiG-31 Firefox, that Clint Eastwood's character, Major Mitchell Gant, is enlisted to steal as part of a joint British/American military effort. /Film listed it as the seventh best of Eastwood's nine war movies, and it's definitely a must-see for any fans of the "Top Gun" films.

Naturally, a plane-based plot requires a lot of aerial scenes involving the fictional title plane that have to be inserted into shots via a matte. Eastwood recalled his VFX issues like this:

"There were so many different ways in which this plane has to fly. And the big difficulty with particular this kind of a film is, all of a sudden, you go to special effects people, and you say, 'Now, this time, we're not out in outer space where nobody knows what it looks like. We're not on a black backdrop so matte lines, etc. etc., all disappear. I want to fly in the clouds and in the planet, and I want to fly over ice, white snow, the Arctic.' And everybody's going, 'Oh my God, there's no way this is going to happen.'"

Clint Eastwood, too, seemed to be alluding to the VFX in "Firefox" in direct comparison with the effects from "Star Wars."

John Dykstra reiterated Eastwood's comment about matte lines by saying that "in space, where everything's black ... that automatically takes care of the problem." He then added that when you do a similar effect against a blue sky, "the bit that turns black between the airplane and the sky is really obnoxious." Luckily, Dykstra handily eliminated said lines using unmentioned VFX alchemy.

Elsewhere in the doc, Dykstra gave an exasperated laugh at the amount of effort that went into capturing the slow-motion shots of the sky, and how little film was used. He said:

"What we did is we went out and shot at slow framerates, meaning two frames or one frame a second. But you must remember something: one frame a second, at the speed we're traveling — 350 miles an hour in a Learjet — we cover, oh, 150 miles in the amount of time it takes to shoot ten seconds of film. So, in fact, you run out of location very quickly at that rate!"

These kinds of VFX issues were likely annoying to Clint Eastwood, as he is notoriously efficient when it comes to his directorial efforts. Eastwood saved "The Bridges of Madison County" from production limbo by essentially asking for 24 hours to begin prep. He usually gets the shots he needs in one or two takes, so his potential annoyance with the meticulous nature of having to wait for special VFX shots for "Firefox" would be understandable.

#3508. Lil’ Kim Takes The Spotlight—With A Symphony

When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as a source of inspiration on your favorite designer’s mood board ever since. On November 18 and 19, to celebrate the music that cemented her icon status, Lil’ Kim will perform in front of a symphony orchestra at the Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, not far from her humble beginnings.

Today she’s less interested in being in the spotlight and more focused on raising her 12-year-old daughter, Royal Reign. In between practices for her performances, Lil’ Kim spoke with Vanity Fair to reflect on her career, how she spends her days, and her standout looks.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: What do you remember about putting your debut album, Hard Core, together?

Lil’ Kim: I remember Biggie and Un [Lance Rivera], who was the label owner that we had. I watched Un build a record label called Undeas, which [stood] for “Un ideas,” and then he finally sold it to Atlantic Records. At the time, we didn’t know the process, but we became Undeas-Atlantic. I remember Biggie having the idea of how he wanted my album to be red, and he explained it to me and Un. I was able to write according to how his idea was to present me, because when they met me, I was who I was—in high heels, jeans, motorcycle jackets, and furs at 13.

Portrait of members of R&B group 112 and rappers Notorious BIG and Lil’ Kim circa 1996

That’s incredible. It sounds like your fashion-icon status started very early. Was there anyone that you looked to back then? What inspired you to dress that way?

My mom was a big inspiration to me when it came to fashion, and so I looked to her for a lot of things. I used to wear her mink coat. She used to wear big sunglasses with her fur coats, with the diamonds and jewelry. She was always taking vacations and I would see her pack her stuff, and she would always have the cutest outfits. They were all matchy-matchy. It’s funny because she would have her outfit to go play tennis in and her outfit would match her tennis racket. So when I bought my big house, I bought a Chanel tennis outfit and I bought the racket to match it, because of my mom.

I love that. Do you keep up with tennis or specifically the ladies in tennis?

No, I haven’t in a while, but, of course, you know, Serena and Venus were like my heroes.

Well, maybe we need to see you on the court one day.

I know. I’m pretty sure I’m rusty, but I like to get out there, though. I used to beat my cousin’s butt back then.

How did the symphony performances come about?

My agents called me and they’re like, “Kim, what do you think?” And I was like, “That’s a freaking awesome idea.” I love performing with bands. And so I imagine that it could be very similar, if not very close. And I thought this could be something really different for me. Sometimes I even listen to classical music. I don’t have to know who the artist is, but I just put on a station and let it flow.

Do you have a favorite song from Hard Core?

I love “Queen Bitch”; it’s my favorite song. It’s still my favorite to perform. And “Crush on You.”

Salma Hayek, Donatella Versace, Pamela Anderson, and Lil’ Kim at Versace’s spring/summer 2001 fashion show

When it comes to fashion, you’re obviously on everyone’s mood board, from stylists to designers, so how important was fashion for you as part of the Lil’ Kim persona?

I just was being myself, honestly. When I first met Biggie, I was coming from my after-school job at Bloomingdale’s. I was probably 13 or 14 at the time, and they would let the teenagers work there.

But I had on a motorcycle jacket and high heels. And one of my best friends told Biggie, “You know, my girl can rap,” because we knew he was rapping around the way. And he was like, “I heard you can rap.” And I just laughed. He was like, “Yeah, see, I knew you didn’t know how to rap.” He was very condescending. He knew how to get you to do what you wanted to do, because I was really shy.

And then I started rapping, and he was blown away because I had on high heels. No one had ever seen someone just bust a rap in high heels. When Biggie, Un, and Jacob York started really talking to me, they didn’t want to change me because that was just what they were so blown away about. That was just who I was.

Do you think people ever misunderstood the way you presented yourself?

To be honest, I never really felt misunderstood by my hardcore fans—the kids my age and the younger kids, they totally got it. I think that’s why I had such a cult following and there was such pandemonium about me when I came out. They understood me. I think it was the older people and the politicians, those are the people who I think misunderstood me.

What did you think of the midterm elections and all of the women who broke barriers in the Senate and gubernatorial offices?

I’m going to be honest with you, I stay away from politics.

Are you keeping up with all of the changes within fashion today? When I listen to your music, you’ve mentioned so many designers and houses, and since then the creative directors have changed. Are you following all of the changes within fashion and seeing how you’re still a part of the conversation?

That’s what I’m trying to say. As a fashion icon, if you really her, and I’m considering myself really her, that’s never gonna change. That’s never going to change. I might put on a fur coat that my stylist or myself will get asked about, because I style myself a lot. And I was styling myself then.

Lil’ Kim and daughter, Royal Reign, on June 16, 2016, in New York City

Extremely rewarding. My daughter’s with me all the time. This world is so cruel and so evil; it’s so different. She’s my safe haven. I feel the extra need to keep her safe.

What does a regular day look like for you?

Lately, I’ve just been really getting into myself. I get up and go have a little spa day. I might take my daughter to go do whatever she wants.

Singer Mary J. Blige with Diana Ross and Lil’ Kim at the 1999 MTV Video Music Awards on September 9, 1999

How do you feel that we’re still talking about your MTV VMAs look in 1999?

I think it’s iconic and I love it. I love when they bring that up, because it was a fun day and it was so good to see people’s faces when they saw my outfit.

Are there any other looks that don’t get as much love as you wish that they did?

I don’t know, because most of the looks that I love, they get the love. There’s a look when I was on the cover of Nylon magazine and I had the teddy bear dress on; that’s one of my favorite looks. The Louis Vuitton look is one of my favorite looks; I love that look. A lot of the Chanel looks and the Versace and the Chanel in the hair.

#3507. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

Kelly Clarkson never fails to entertain or make me emotional on The Voice. I enjoy seeing her bring out the heartfelt words of encouragement, maybe even more than I enjoy watching her attempt to steal country singers from Riley Green. (But only slightly.) She never shies away from tearing up, or channeling what she learned from her American Idol days, which is what she used to give advice to contestants whenever The Voice goes live.

Something about the way the singer digs deep into the emotions really hits home. The Clarkson's advice may be a little "dark" as she reminds contestants to live in every moment, but there’s also something beautifully human about it. Clarkson is possibly influenced by the passing of her ex-husband Brandon Blackstock when she reminds her team that life is short. She shares with People ahead of The Voice’s live shows in early November what she tells contestants:

I know this sounds dark and I don’t mean it to. I mean it to sound so beautiful and in the moment and present, but you just don’t know how long you have on this planet. We’re artists, enjoy the moment. You might mess up and that’s OK, as long as people want to watch people being incredible at what they do.

Clarkson knows exactly what they’re experiencing. Not only did she go through a similar competition on American Idol, but she often performs live at concerts, events, and even during her former show’s “Kellyoke” segments. This is part of the reason her talk show was so popular, even winning multiple daytime Emmys for outstanding series.

While Clarkson has definitely upped her zany antics, including trying to give a contestant her hair, she’s also continues to bring the emotions. There’s always at least one singer who brings Clarkson (and the rest of us) to tears, and it all has to do with her appreciation for experiencing every moment. That’s exactly what she wants her team to know, even if it makes her sound like a mom:

I didn’t want them to be so nervous. It sounds really cheesy but really being present in the moment like, ‘Hey this is a really special thing that you’re getting to do right now. Really take that in.’ I’m such a mom.

As a mom of two, this has likely impacted her outlook on competition, especially when it comes to younger contestants like 13-year-old Brianna Cameron. Though who didn't share a tear during "Inseparable"? However, it’s not all emotional on The Voice as Clarkson reminds us yet again why she may just be the funniest Coach.... even if this season gave her some humorous competition. Whether it’s engaging in some smack talk with her fellow coaches or upping the goofy hijinks, it’s obvious she’s having a good time.

Season 30 has been a blast, and it’s largely due to the four coaches, which includes Adam Levine and newbie coaches Queen Latifah and Riley Green. However, while I’ve enjoyed the zany zingers and even the duck blind prank, it’s the emotional moments and performances that seem to land a little harder.

You can watch new episodes of The Voice every Monday on NBC and the next day with a Peacock subscription. The season is quickly winding down with the finale just around the corner on December 14.

#3505. Robert Pattinson's James Bond Gives The Franchise An Opportunity It's Never Had Before

After well over a year of rampant speculation, Amazon MGM Studios and director Denis Villeneuve have found their James Bond, and it's Robert Pattinson. As many have noted, Pattinson's casting as Bond marks the first time an established movie star has been brought on to play 007 (Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan were TV stars prior to earning their license to kill), and some folks are lamenting that the fun of a Bond transition is getting to watch an actor grow into the role. Pattinson, however, offers moviegoers a different opportunity: Just how will this actor, who's renowned for playing weirdos and affecting strange accents, approach a character who hasn't exhibited much of a sense of humor since Roger Moore surrendered his Walther PPK in 1985?

Pattinson's run as Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" movies led many to underestimate him as an actor. He played the vampire Edward Cullen as a brooding emo teenager (though he's actually 104 years old), and, at least until Bill Condon came on to direct the final two installments, the films generally didn't ask much of him. He also might've hurt himself with his portrayal of a young Salvador Dali in 2008's "Little Ashes," where his interesting physical and vocal choices are undone by a perfectly awful Spanish accent.

But once he got clear of "Twilight," Pattinson began flaunting his versatility in films like David Cronenberg's "Cosmopolis," David Michôd's "The Rover" (where he's deeply moving as a twitchy southerner who can't take care of himself), and Josh and Bennie Safdie's "Good Time" (which lets him cut loose as a low-level New York City criminal). No actor has stepped into the role of Bond with as varied a resume as this. And it only gets more varied the further along you read.

One of Robert Pattinson's zaniest performances can be found in David and Nathan Zellner's "Damsel," a dark Western comedy where he plays an eccentric pioneer who speaks in a high-pitched twang. He's an overbearing type who's not nearly as smart or entertaining as he thinks he is. Contrast this with his sublime turn as a tormented sea dog in Robert Eggers' "The Lighthouse." There, Pattinson makes for a weathered, sour delight as a lighthouse keeper who detests his tyrannical superior (Willem Dafoe) — the same chap who happens to be his only companion in this Maine lighthouse (circa 1890).

If you're looking for hints as to how Pattinson might play James Bond, he's conventionally charming and suave as agent Neil in Christopher Nolan's "Tenet," yet he plays Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' "The Batman" as more of an aloof and dour oddball than most other actors have. If Denis Villeneuve wants a dark and brooding 007, then Pattinson's Caped Crusader might be a helpful point of reference.

For those hoping that Villeneuve might lighten up the James Bond franchise, look at his filmography. It's highly unlikely he'll let Pattinson yuk it up à la Roger Moore. But nowadays, it seems like Pattinson can't help but make interesting choices. (Just look at his 2026 trifecta of "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime.") He's one of our most interesting stars, and it would be a shame if Villeneuve played it safe and had him do Daniel Craig redux. I think that's also unlikely, but if the filmmaker could let Pattinson sprinkle some behavioral quirks into the part, we could have our most interesting Bond ... well, ever.

#3504. The Odyssey's Most Disturbing Scene Barely Used Any CGI. Here's How They Pulled It Off.

Christopher Nolan and his team reveals how silicone, magnets, and Samantha Morton's performance brought a disturbing transformation to life.

Christopher Nolan and his team reveals how silicone, magnets, and Samantha Morton's performance brought a disturbing transformation to life.

She led them in, sat them on chairs, and blended them a potion of barley, cheese, and golden honey, mixed with Pramnian wine. She added potent drugs to make them totally forget their home. They took and drank the mixture. Then she struck them, using her magic wand, and penned them in the pigsty. They were turned to pigs in body and voice and hair; their minds remained the same. — The Odyssey, Emily Wilson translation

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17, giving audiences another opportunity to experience the filmmaker's ambitious adaptation of Homer's epic poem. Among the story's many memorable encounters is Circe, a powerful sorceress who turns Odysseus' men into pigs. Played by Samantha Morton, Circe is responsible for one of the film's most unsettling sequences, which involves a human head being transformed into that of a pig.

It's the kind of effect you'd assume required extensive computer-generated imagery. As it turns out, the filmmakers accomplished almost the entire transformation using practical effects, some silicone, and a few strategically placed magnets.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson and special effects supervisor Scott Fisher explain how the sequence came together, revealing that the secret wasn't some elaborate digital trick. Instead, it was finding a way to let Morton perform the transformation herself.

I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced.

Emma Thomas, Nolan's wife and longtime producing partner, admits that several moments in the screenplay left her wondering how they could possibly be accomplished, but the Circe sequence stood out.

"I loved that sequence when I read it, and I knew he wanted to make it feel very grounded," Thomas tells Polygon. "I knew that he wanted to try and do it with makeup effects to the extent that he could."

Thomas wasn't initially sure how that would work, particularly given the limitations she assumed existed with practical makeup effects.

"I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced," she says.

Her confidence grew once she began meeting with the makeup, special effects, and visual effects teams, including makeup and creature effects artist Conor O'Sullivan.

"That was the point at which I really realized: Oh my goodness, these guys are gonna come up with a way that each can contribute their talents and their skills with the best of technology from within their own disciplines and make a seamless sequence."

Of course, getting there required a little trial and error.

According to Jackson, the team knew early on that the key to the sequence would be allowing Morton to physically interact with the heads and manipulate their transformation.

"We had various ways that we were gonna try and achieve that, with heads with kind of clay layers that she could manipulate," Jackson says.

They even built some of those early versions, but the results weren't particularly promising. The transformation took too long, making the effect difficult to incorporate into the scene.

"We both were looking at it and going, 'Yeah, that's not really gonna work in Chris's world,'" Jackson recalled.

Rather than abandon the practical approach, the team came up with a different solution, working alongside O'Sullivan to develop a skull beneath a layer of soft silicone skin. The idea was that Morton could manipulate the skull through the skin, physically changing the shape of the head. But O'Sullivan had another trick up his sleeve.

"Conor came up with this great idea of having it pre-broken and stuck back together with magnets so she could do whatever kind of manipulation she wanted to and just keep going," Jackson says.

The skull was already separated into pieces, with magnets holding everything together. That allowed Morton to squeeze and reshape the head as part of her performance, rather than wait for a complicated mechanical effect to do the work. And because the prop didn't require constant resetting, Morton could continue performing without interruption.

"The idea that there was no resetting, so no kind of breaking her performance, was why that scene was so compelling," Jackson says. "She just had this prop that she could really go to town on."

For an effect involving a human head becoming a pig's, giving an actor that kind of freedom might sound like a strange creative priority. But it meant the transformation wasn't simply something happening to a character through movie magic. Morton was physically making it happen.

"Ultimately, in what ended up in the film, there is very little visual effects affecting what was actually shot," Jackson says.

The visual effects team made some adjustments, including manipulating the eyeballs to make their movements more frantic. Jackson also notes that an ear transformation required combining two camera angles and slight of hand. But the majority of the sequence was accomplished in-camera.

"Essentially all our involvement was prior to the shoot, and then once the shoot happened, that was kind of it in camera," Jackson says. The visual effects team wasn't absent from the process. Its expertise helped develop the practical solution in the first place.

It's also consistent with Nolan's broader filmmaking philosophy, and the director notes that even sequences requiring visual effects benefit from capturing as much real material as possible.

"Even where we know we're absolutely gonna have to avail ourselves of visual effects, really try to give the compositors as much as possible to work with," Nolan tells Polygon. In the case of Circe's transformation, that collaboration resulted in an effect that required very little digital assistance once filming was complete.

For Thomas, the finished sequence demonstrates just how much could be accomplished when different effects departments combine their expertise. What initially seemed like one of the screenplay's biggest technical challenges became an example of practical and digital artists working together to find a solution.

And for audiences revisiting The Odyssey at home, the sequence offers something worth examining a little more closely. Beneath all that unsettling movie magic is a surprisingly straightforward idea: a silicone-covered skull held together with magnets, and an actress given the freedom to do the rest.

The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17

#3503. Stacey Abrams in Conversation With Ta-Nehisi Coates

When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue. This struck me as unlikely. But three years later Abrams ran for governor, and shocked the country by coming within two points of winning. Then two years later, when Joe Biden sealed his presidential election in 2020 with a win in Georgia, and Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff won Senate seats, Abrams looked prophetic. Now, Democrats have gone beyond Georgia, penetrating into the deepest reaches of the South—Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. To understand how the GOP’s Solid South grew brittle, I could think of no better person to talk to than Abrams.

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me. You interviewed me for the book. We had a wonderful discussion. My family was actually in the audience, because, like all Black folks, I have family in Atlanta. They were so excited. I was talking to Stacey Abrams—Minority Leader Stacey Abrams. And one of the things you said backstage was, “We’re going to make Georgia blue.” And I don’t know that I scoffed at you. I like to think I wasn’t quite that rude.

Stacey Abrams: Your eyebrow arched a bit.

I confess to the eyebrow arching. And so the eyebrow arched and you made the case. Can you tell me what you saw?

I’d gone through redistricting, and one of the component pieces of redistricting, of course, is that it’s predicated on the census. The US census is a tool that is incredibly powerful and deeply inexact. It was the first time Republicans had power to draw the lines since Reconstruction. And I took a posture in my caucus, and it was this: “If you vote for their maps, I will come after your seats.” And I was not only unequivocal in saying it, I wrote it down because I didn’t want anyone to misquote me.

In order to take that posture, I had to read the maps myself. And what I saw was that Republicans were placing bets that, by drawing the lines a certain way, they were going to give themselves 124 of 180 seats. So 67% of the seats, even though they’d only won the election by 57%.

But I looked at those same maps and I’m like, In this place, in this part of Paulding County, there is a new subdivision that is predominantly Black. And in this part of Gwinnett County, there is a burgeoning Korean population that is now going into its second generation, which means a lot of those will be eligible voters. And down in South Georgia, you have third-generation migrant farm workers who are Latino, but who have decided to plant their roots here and raise their families here. When you looked at those numbers, the maps had a very different story to tell about Republican dominance: They could win for a decade. They could not win for a generation.

We tell ourselves stories about the information we get, and people repeat stories without ever reading it themselves. There are a lot of people who can quote Tom Sawyer who’ve never read the book. And so in our politics, that happens a lot, that the story that becomes popular doesn’t ever get traced back to its origin or to the original text.

What I saw in Georgia is true in Louisiana, in Mississippi, in Tennessee, in Alabama, in South Carolina. We just saw it happen in North Carolina.

So when you saw this wave of redistricting happening around the country this year, did you see a similar opportunity?

Oh, absolutely. I was in Tennessee the day that they passed the maps and what stuck out for me was Raumesh Akbari, who’s the Senate minority leader, she asked to see the bill, and the Republican chair of the committee said, “Well, we don’t have a bill yet, but we know what it’s going to say.” They planned to vote on it even though they did not have the text of the bill.

The Republicans were moving so fast because they thought they understood what they were pulling together. Justin Pearson didn’t pick up the seat he wanted, but they were at risk of losing a seat they thought was going to be theirs because they misread the topography, but they didn’t do a deeper dive into exactly what was laying in the crevices. And that’s where opportunity for us is born.

There are not enough Black people to win any single seat outright on their own in most legislative districts, and no statewide elections, especially post–Louisiana v. Callais, but there are coalitions that can be built. And what I saw from the very beginning was the possibility of coalition.

What I see for the South, what I think the South proved on Tuesday, is the possibility of coalition, but coalition does not happen without conflict. It does not happen without conversation, and it does not happen when we have convinced ourselves of the permanence of our second-class citizenship and our subjugation. What we saw on Tuesday was a moment where people realized that the power to improve their own lives had become so desperately thin that they had to use it or lose it. We cannot rely on that for the next two years.

What I hear you saying is that the last two years created an emergency. But that can’t be depended on. It can’t be “The Most Important Election of Our Lifetime” every two years. Desperation is not enough.

It can’t be. Desperation gets you one moment. There’s a whole body of medical research on people that have heart attacks and they get saved. And what it shows is that they are exercise fiends for about six weeks and then they fall back into their patterns because it’s a normalcy bias.

If we constantly feel on the edge of danger, we cannot function. And so we reorient our understanding of normal to survive. And therefore our responsibility in this moment is to look at the opportunity that was revealed on Tuesday, but not read into it that that opportunity either requires desperation or it requires this milquetoast approach, because our default is not just normalcy, but the most banal form of normalcy we can imagine.

I know you have some concerns about some of the narratives emerging out of the midterms. Would you talk a bit about that?

I saw something on Axios that I think was well-intentioned and it essentially said that the threats to our democracy were overblown, that our courts held, that our Congress held, that our presidency wasn’t overreaching, and that for normal people, things were fine. How have we reached the place where we think it is normal that the capital city in the United States of America is under military occupation? How is it okay that the courts held when it permits the incarceration of children in Dilley, Texas, and the kidnapping of people of color because of race and the language that they speak? There is something aggressively privileged about this idea that democracy is not in jeopardy because those who are the most protected don’t feel harm.

But Tuesday was a repudiation of this idea that things are normal. You saw turnout at extraordinary levels from a cross section of communities, almost all of whom have been directly impacted by the harms of this administration. Not just the economic harms that hit everyone, but harms that were amplified and refined for their cruelty.

At the same time, there’s a worry that I have that, because we won control of Congress for the patriots—and that’s how I frame it, I no longer think it’s just Democrat versus Republican, it’s patriots versus authoritarians—even though the patriots may have gained more purchase in Congress, we still have a Supreme Court that gutted the last vestiges of protection for the Voting Rights Act. We still have a Supreme Court that stripped women of their bodily autonomy. We still have a Supreme Court that has said that protections that are afforded by DEI are somehow suspect. And when those are true, then the successes of Tuesday don’t signal that we’ve won. They signal that we have to work even harder because the harms have not dissipated, they just haven’t penetrated.

You said something a few months back that’s stuck with me—that our elections are ripe for entertainment. As a sports fan, I think it’s not a coincidence that so many sports figures are now commenting on politics because the way they appear on TV is actually quite similar to the way sports appears. You have these long campaigns, which is like your season. Then you have primaries, which are like your playoffs, and then you have this big Super Bowl that happens on Tuesday. And so, it’s an entertainment and ratings bonanza. And I think, as I recall, you were cautioning against that as a view of politics. Can you speak a little bit more about that?

Yeah. When you think about politics, if you think about elections as an event, and to extend your analogy, if the elections are the finals, if the elections are game seven, if it’s the Super Bowl, when that happens, then the day after, you go home, the game is over. But the challenge I have is that it’s not just that we treat it as a sporting event, it’s that we treat politics as though we are spectators at a sporting event. And when we look at the other party, it’s like we are spectators watching a very disciplined, seasoned team that practices in the off-season, that travels together, that plays overseas. They’re constantly engaged and we are on and off. We think of politics, again, as entertainment as opposed to the job.

How did we end up with this entertainment narrative?

Theodore White did this series where he examined elections 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972. And when you read it, as someone who is reading it in the 21st century, the arc of how we have viewed politics changed dramatically, specifically in 1960 with the advent of television, because the election contest between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon hinged in no small part on that televised debate. And I think for you and me and for anyone who wasn’t old enough to see it, I did not realize that it was one of the most watched programs in American history. We take for granted how many people are going to watch the debates these days, but with that first debate, it was one of the most watched programs in the world because it had never happened before. And the moment it became a television spectacle, it became entertainment because you were watching, you picked winners and losers, you picked your villain and you picked your champion.

It’s human nature, we put things into these narrative arcs. As someone who writes comic books, you understand this. As someone who writes thrillers, I think about this. You create a villain, you have a protagonist, an antagonist, you have to have a storyline, you have to have complications, and when television became the medium, it added a layer and a texture to what had long been the mechanics of politics. Then you add into it the drama of Black and brown people getting to participate. And then you layer on top of that “blue state versus red state,” and the sharp division, and the attribution to entire regions of a value system and a personality based on a single day.

What would it mean to remain engaged beyond elections? When I think about the conservative movement, I think about the degree to which the religious right is engaged. I think about Trump rallies. I think people were baffled by this at first—the clothes, the trucks, the boats. But what I would say is those are markers of community. They aren’t my politics. But they seem part of something larger than a particular bill or policy.

There’s a lot of talk in organizing about going for belief first, or belonging first. On the left, we are often accused of belief, that you have to be in line with all of our ideas, our values, our ideologies, but also the tactical, practical ways of exercising them, and that because we say you have to believe first, we filter out people who haven’t had time to understand or adapt or even decide what they believe. The right uses belonging. They say, “Come and be a part of us, and we’ll tell you what we are.” So you get the jersey, you get the cap, you get the red, you get to use the language, even if you haven’t decided that you actually believe all they believe, which is why you have people who are suddenly surprised that this is what happened.

We have to shift. Not to say that we don’t have beliefs, but we have to give people time to grow into those beliefs. I come at this from my time as minority leader. I had a caucus of 60 members in a chamber of 180, and my members included suburban white mothers and rural Black pastors and everything in between. We were the most racially diverse caucus. We were geographically diverse. And I had no power. I was the minority leader. My job was to help harmonize their approach. I could not lead with belief, because people were entitled to their beliefs, but my job was to bring them into belonging first because they were members of the caucus. And then my second job was to make sure that anyone who needed them to believe something had the platform to offer the tutelage.

That’s the place where I think we are failing. We don’t do the tutelage. We say, “There has been a conversation, this is now our truth. And if you don’t adopt that truth, you are somehow opposed to it,” as opposed to, “You haven’t adopted the truth because you don’t know what it means and you don’t understand it and you haven’t experienced it. Let me give you time and space to come in,” or, “You have legitimate disagreement, and maybe on this, we will not be in alignment, but your disagreement should not lead to hostility against my community.”

The Democratic Socialists of America have attracted a lot of attention recently, but one thing they seem to do is this “belonging” piece. I can’t say I understood this before, but I was talking to someone for a story, and then mentioned the social environment. So here in New York, when people go out to canvas, afterwards, they all go out for beers. The beers are not really the point, but making people feel like they belong to something is.

Yeah. I mean, what they are doing is what works in most effective social movements. During the Vietnam War, one of the most effective protest waves happened at coffee shops. You brought people together around the table, they got to vent about what they were upset about, they went out and protested and then they came back together. People like being liked.

In terms of belief, how does one do that and not make those who are in that coalition who are particularly vulnerable feel abandoned? Obviously, I mean, this is not the only case, but I’m thinking about the tremendous amount of negative attention brought on the trans community. What do you do when the “belonging” comes in conflict with actually protecting the members of your coalition?

My first position is, if you have a faith that tells you it is okay to cause harm because you feel uncomfortable, I need to understand where your faith lies. Our first responsibility is the protection of difference. And it is to say you don’t have to embrace, but you cannot lift up pitchforks. You cannot demonize, you cannot revile, you cannot scapegoat because all of those are hostile actions of cruelty that not only cause harm to the victim, they diminish your ability to learn. So the worry I have is that too often we sacrifice that education piece because it’s uncomfortable and because it requires defending those you may not be in complete alignment with, and it’s an easier thing to just jump on the bandwagon.

In my caucus, when I was a minority leader, another issue I had was abortion, and I had two members who were pastors. I was not going to be able to change their ideological position and I wasn’t going to try. But I had these members walk off the floor, instead of voting, on abortion bills. And there were some who got mad and they’re like, “Oh, we should know their position.” I said, “A yes vote on this bill causes harm, and no vote is a help. Not voting is the same as a no vote. So why do you need them to make a declaration when their declaration of refusing to do harm is progress?” So there’s a complexity that we often elide because we failed to measure what harm looks like, and the path from good to harm is a lot shorter than we want to believe.

Did you work with Angie Nixon during her race?

I feel like she excited a certain element of the base in a way that we haven’t really seen before.

I contributed and then I went down to Florida, actually did an event at Florida A&M University and did one at Cafe Resistance. I got to know her mama. I traveled with her some. I knew of her as a state representative. And when I decided to support her campaign, it was because she has always put the work of serving people first. She has built networks, but more importantly, she solves problems.

When Florida started banning books, she started a bookstore for banned books. That kind of tactical response with strategic intention is often lacking and it has been part of how I try to operate. We’ve got people who are good at being diagnosticians and we’ve got folks who can offer prescriptions and we’ve got people who can actually administer the medicine. And we need more people who are willing to do all three. You need people who are specialists; I’m not saying you don’t, but what she has demonstrated is the capacity to do the three.

Have you heard some of the negative commentary after the election about her campaign? I’m thinking about James Carville, for instance—this notion that somehow she was a poor fit for Florida or was a bad candidate. It’s not great. Have you seen any of this?

Well, I have thoughts on the fact that we keep thinking the solution to the problem is the thing that failed before. And I believe in experimentation. If you look at my history, I have never been top of mind as the solution to problems. And some of it is timing, some of it is capacity, and some of it is helping change the public imagination, but we’re never going to get what we need if we only use what we’ve always had.

I just find it interesting that she is attracting negative commentary, from certain quarters, in a way that David Jolly is not, even though they both lost and the margin wasn’t that much between the two of them. She came very, very close to winning, in a state Democrats really didn’t expect to compete in two years ago. And look, I just have to say, you are somebody who in 2018 came really, really close too. You’re both Black women. I just wonder what you make of the critique.

The critique is easy because Angie Nixon is different. She’s different than what they are used to, and she is different than 250 years of expectation has led us to presume is right. I am excited about Juliana Stratton and Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester being in the US Senate. That is an extraordinary thing. Adding Angie Nixon would’ve been an amazing, amazing addition. But for pundits whose sense of success is grounded in past history, she strains the imagination.

David Jolly ran a smart race. Angie Nixon ran a smart race, and we know that because they came close to winning, but you are never entitled to victory. You are entitled to effort. And this notion that there is some magical formula for what wins in the South got completely obliterated yesterday when Scott Colom won a seat that we haven’t held since 1874. We know that what can win is a combination of a smart candidate, an invested campaign, and an electorate who sees and hears themselves in the story told.

Angie didn’t get that opportunity because she had a late primary and no resources. And to judge her using a metric that was never designed for her is deeply problematic. And it’s not just about her being a Black woman, it’s about how do we win an evolving electorate if all we know is to do what we’ve always done? And so my argument for the Democratic Party is that our notions of electability have to evolve with the democracy that we deserve and that we design, and it cannot be anchored to these sometimes antiquated notions that the only thing we can do is not lose as opposed to let’s try really hard to win by meeting the moment. And I think Angie Nixon did an incredible job of meeting the moment.

And what about you—do you still have ambitions for public office?

Do you worry that some of the work you do as a kind of public political strategist (like in this interview, frankly) will conflict at all? When I think about people seeking office, they often try to say as little as possible.

Politics is a tool. It is not an identity for me. It’s a tool. And that’s different. And there are people for whom this is what they do and we need those people. This is not a disparaging comment about others, but for me, it is a tool. It is one of the ways to do the work I believe needs to be done. I think that poverty is immoral. I think it is solvable. I think it is economically inefficient. And for most of my life, the work for me has been about how do you solve this economic poverty? When I got deep in the work, I realized that we also had a moral poverty that we had to contend with, and we have this poverty of imagination. And the problem is you cannot convince people to believe that their problems can be solved if you won’t talk about them.

And in the South, silence is protective. It has been a way to nibble around the edges, but the only people who could be loud about it were the people who could afford volume. And politicians rarely can afford volume. I want things to be better and I’m not willing to forgo any tool that will make that happen. But I’m also not willing to protect my future opportunities by rejecting my current responsibilities.

Woot has dropped the price of the JBL PartyBox 330 to $479.95 as an early Black Friday deal, saving you $150 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Beyond the discount, the PartyBox 330 has plenty to offer if you're looking for a speaker that can handle everything from backyard barbecues to larger gatherings—sitting between the smaller Club 120 and the larger PartyBox 520 in JBL's lineup, it delivers deep, punchy bass and enough volume to entertain a crowd, while its roughly 20-hour battery life means you can keep the music going all day without having to find an outlet. That protection has limits, though—the 330 isn’t dustproof or particularly impact-resistant, so you’ll still want to be careful where you set it down. #3501. The Downfall Of Sony's Spider-Man Universe Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

If Marvel Comics has proved anything over the past 63 years, it's that the number of stories you can tell about Spider-Man is essentially infinite. Not only is he a great character in his own right, he also has an incredible roster of villains and one of the best supporting casts in the history of superhero comics. And yet, despite the success of movies about the web-slinging wall-crawler himself, Sony Pictures' attempts to expand into a full-on Spider-Man Universe have been, to put it bluntly, an abysmal failure on virtually every level.

With Sony scrapping plans for expanding into more villain-focused films, moviegoers are left with burning questions. How could a cinematic franchise built around characters like Madame Web and Morbius possibly have failed? Who could have predicted that audiences might not care about the origin of Kraven the Hunter's cool jacket as much as they care about him, say, fighting Spider-Man? Was the world ever going to be ready for Morbin' Time? It's nearly impossible to say for sure, but upon examining the timeline of Sony's many attempts to get their Spidey-themed side universe going, one thing becomes apparent: It all went wrong with 2018's "Venom" — not because it was bad, but because it was good.

Under normal circumstances, a superhero movie being good would be the furthest thing from a problem, even if it might seem like an unlikely success. 1998's "Blade," after all, took its title vampire hunter from a C-list character to a surprise hit, becoming Marvel's first brush with cinematic success years before the X-Men and Spider-Man hit the big screen. That proved that with a strong enough vision, a character could be taken out of the context of a traditional story and work just as well — or in Blade's case, even better.

It's hard not to look at "Venom" as a sort of cinematic descendant of "Blade." Both movies took a darker approach to superhero storytelling and mixed in a heaping helping of genre conventions to keep things feeling fresh — vampire horror for "Blade," and classic alien invasion sci-fi for "Venom." There are, however, some pretty significant differences. For one, unlike the pre-movie version of Blade, Venom had a much stronger track record of being a fan-favorite character who could stand on his own, even with his unbreakable ties to Spider-Man. For another, while "Blade" was definitely a hit, the success of "Venom" absolutely blows it out of the vampire-infested water. Thanks largely to Tom Hardy's incredibly charismatic performance as both Eddie Brock and his alien symbiote BFF, "Venom" racked up a staggering $856 million at the box office.

"Venom" brought in a ton of money, garnered acclaim from critics and fans, and seemed to be proof of concept that characters related to Spider-Man can carry a film without him. For a company looking to build its own superhero franchise juggernaut (or at least a franchise Rhino) with a suite of characters whose rights its been hanging onto for over 20 years, that's good news, right? Well ... not if you're determined to learn the wrong lesson.

While we'll never really know what was going through the minds of the studio executives who thought releasing "Morbius" twice was a good idea, it's easy to imagine how a thought process that's more concerned with the bottom line than with storytelling and character might interpret the massive success of "Venom." If that movie can succeed by featuring a Spider-Man villain on his own without Spider-Man involved at all, then why can't all these other characters that came along when Sony got the Spidey rights? These characters are pretty much all the same, right? One's as good as any other.

Unfortunately for Sony, that's not exactly how it works. Villains, particularly Spider-Man's roster of sinister foes, are built to work in the context of their heroic counterparts, and the same usually goes for the supporting cast that orbits around them. It's the contrast and context that makes them interesting. Venom works in a starring role because he's been the protagonist of his own stories for far longer than he was a pure villain. Kraven the Hunter, on the other hand, doesn't have that development. Weirdly enough, the character who probably had the best shot at standing on their own was Morbius, who is only tangentially related to Spider-Man and has a history of starring in his own stories, albeit with very little success. Alas, it turns out that sometimes, you actually have to make a good movie, and "Morbius" is anything but that.

Of course, trying to make a Spider-Man universe without Spider-Man was only one of several baffling choices Sony made with its attempted franchise. If any executive had bothered to ask literally anyone who reads comics or knows about superheroes if they should make a movie about Morbius or Madame Web, they would've found out just from the facial expression they were met with that this was a terrible idea. Her web may connect us all, but it certainly wasn't going to connect with audiences.

It’s hard to believe it’s been over 14 years since audiences first saw Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen volunteer as tribute for the 74th Hunger Games. While so much time has passed, that series of book-to-screen adaptations remains greatly loved by fans. Lawrence herself seems to have an appreciation for that time in her life as well even if it wasn’t always easy for her to control the craziness. Ahead of her return as Katniss, Lawrence shared a sweet throwback pic of herself with two of her key co-stars, and her caption is great.

Lawrence is set to play Katniss for the first time in over a decade in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which is set to hit the 2026 movie schedule in a matter of days. It would seem that the Oscar winner is feeling a bit nostalgic, as she recently took to her Instagram stories to share some classic pics, possibly from press tours from the early aughts. One particularly sweet photo shows Lawrence alongside Peeta Mellark actor Josh Hutcherson and Gale Hawthorne star Liam Hemsworth. Check out it below:

The mere sight of this lovely photo is enough to hit someone with a hearty helping of early 2010s nostalgia. I can still remember the sheer amount of buzz that surrounded the release of the first Hunger Games movie adapted from Suzanne Collins’ beloved book series. What we see in that picture are the smiling faces of three people in the midst of an amazing professional journey. Also, leave it to “J. Law” to choose such a cheeky caption for the photo and, let’s be real, the statement isn’t untrue either.

What I really want to know is when exactly this photo was taken. I mean, was this taken around the time the OG film in the young adult franchise came out or at a later date. Regardless, I appreciate Lawrence sharing such sweet mementos, and you can check out another post down below. This one features two black-and-white photos — one of the trio hanging out on what appears to be a bridge and another shot of them on a bed:

Jennifer Lawrence is practically revered for her role as Katniss at this point, as many still hold her performance in high regard, including others who’ve since joined the franchise. Earlier this year, Sunrise on the Reaping’s Maya Hawke praised Lawrence for her character’s impact on the action genre. Ironically, Lawrence explained years ago that she was scared to sign on for the movies, given such blockbusters can “make or break a career.” I think it’s safe to say that everything turned out fine, though.

Josh Hutcherson has also expressed warm feelings about the reception he’s received for his performance as Peeta, which has blown fans away. Though Hutcherson had been away from the franchise for some time, he admitted last fall that he felt a bit of FOMO over not being a part of the newer films. That has changed, however, as Hutcherson is reprising Peeta alongside Lawrence’s Katniss and Woody Harrelson’s (older) Haymitch Abernathy in the latest installment.

How exactly that aforementioned trio of actors factors into this prequel film is unclear at the moment. Nevertheless, I’m sure fans are just pleased that they’ll be returning in some kind of capacity. For now, though, I just find it lovely that Jennifer Lawrence is embracing her memories, and I hope she and the “girls” are able to somehow make some new ones down the road.

Check out The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping when it opens in theaters on November 20. In the meantime, stream the original four films now with a Peacock subscription, or check them out for free on Tubi.

#3499. Everything You Missed at Vanity Fair's Screening Room Los Angeles

Not even a nationwide FAA ground stop could prevent movie stars from descending upon Los Angeles for the Governor Awards and Vanity Fair's first annual Screening Room this past weekend. Hosted at LACMA's brand-new Steve Tisch theater, actors including Matt Damon, Penélope Cruz, Pedro Pascal, Andrew Garfield, John Leguizamo, and Andrew Scott joined Q&As to discuss their films and pressing topics in the entertainment industry. AI was a major theme throughout the weekend, and not just at the screening for Artificial, as actors and directors spoke about the desire to continue making things that feel “real” and “made by humans.” Following each screening, talent mingled with guests to continue the conversations.

The weekend began with a screening of Wild Horse Nine, director Martin McDonagh's dark comedy starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973. Following the showing, VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford led a Q&A with McDonagh, Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, who also stars in the film.

Next up was Elsinore, which tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (played by Andrew Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. In conversation with VF's Rebecca Ford, Scott, his costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, Scott discussed what it was like to tell Charleson's story. “I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” he said.

Come Friday night, audiences gathered for a screening of the acclaimed Spanish language drama La Bola Negra, which follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. It stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

After the film, Ricky Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo talked about how they are all riding high on the film's positive reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”

Saturday's slate of programming began with a live recording of Vanity Fair's “Notes on a Scene” with Matt Damon, John Leguizamo and Himesh Patel, who recounted what it was like to film The Odyssey with director Christopher Nolan. Next, Seth Rogen joined Screening Room for “Scene Selection,” taking the audience through what it was like shooting Freaks and Geeks, Knocked Up, The Studio and more.

Later that afternoon, Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy joined the festivities following a screening of their new film Behemoth!, which tells the story of a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and to score films after decades performing symphonic work around the country. In conversation with VF's West Coast Editor John Ross for Behemoth!, Pascal spoke about how making the film gave him “a tremendous amount of hope.” “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious," he said.

Come Saturday night, guests were eager to see Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, which follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation with VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci. “It's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs,” Garfield said.

On Sunday, Cruz joined director Florian Zeller for a screening of the film Bunker, a timely film about a famous architect, played by Javier Bardem, and his wife Sofia, played by Cruz, who is asked to build a bunker for a tech giant. This sparks a rift in their marriage as the couple examines how success and monetary gain have affected their lives. Cruz, who is having a huge year with The Invite and La Bola Negra alongside this film, expressed her excitement that younger audiences are coming back to theaters and are looking for films that don't “over-explain."

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room paired this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that included post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3498. Samsung’s Newest Flagship Soundbar System Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.
